# 1. Introduction to R

R is a programming language and software environment used for statistical computing, data analysis, and data visualization.
```{r calculator}
# Basic calculations
20 + 10
50 - 8
30 * 20
90 / 3
6^4
```

# 2. Data structures in R

## 2.1 Vectors

A vector stores values of the same basic type.

```{r vectors}
# Numeric vector
study_hours <- c(2.5, 3, 4, 1.5, 5)
summary(study_hours)

# Calculate the average study time
mean(study_hours)

# Logical vector
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

# Character vector
students <- c("Marcellin", "Muhoza", "Alice", "Josianne")

# Integer vector
days <- 1:7

# Complex vector
complex_values <- c(4 + 2i, 3 + 2i)

# Check the type of a vector
class(study_hours)
```

## 2.2 Matrices

A matrix stores data in rows and columns. All its values should have the same basic type.

```{r matrices}
# Create a matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns
x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
x

# Create another matrix
y <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
y

# Multiply the two matrices
x %*% y
```

## 2.3 Lists

A list can store different types of values together.

```{r lists}
# Create a list with different types of information
student_info <- list(
  name = "Marcellin",
  age = 25,
  registered = TRUE,
  score = 80 + 2i
)

student_info

# Access the student's name
student_info[[1]]
```

## 2.4 Factors

A factor is used to represent categories.

```{r factors}
# Record whether students completed an assignment
assignment_status <- factor(
  c("Completed", "Completed", "Not completed", "Completed", "Not completed")
)

assignment_status
levels(assignment_status)
```

## 2.5 Missing values

R uses `NA` to represent missing information.

```{r missing-values}
# Create a vector with one missing value
scores <- c(60, 84, NA, 85, 78)

# Identify the missing value
is.na(scores)

# Remove missing values when calculating the average
mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r complete-cases}
# Check which rows have complete information
height <- c(160, 155, NA, 140, 185)
weight <- c(68, 58, 70, NA, 70)

complete.cases(height, weight)
```

## 2.6 Coercion

R converts values to a common type when different types are combined in one vector.

```{r coercion}
# Numbers become characters when text is included
mixed_values <- c(10, 20, "thirty")
mixed_values

# TRUE is counted as 1 and FALSE as 0
sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))
```

# 3. Creating a data frame

A data frame stores different types of information in separate columns.

```{r create-data}
# Create information about five students
student_id <- 1:5
student_name <- c("Eric", "Aline", "Patrick", "Diane", "Claude")
height <- c(170, 165, 180, 158, 175)
weight <- c(65, 58, 78, 52, 72)
gender <- c("M", "F", "M", "F", "M")

# Combine the columns into one data frame
student_data <- data.frame(
  student_id, student_name, gender, height, weight
)

student_data
```

## 3.1 Entering data manually

You can also create an empty data frame and enter information using R's editor.

```{r manual-data, eval=FALSE}
# Create an empty data frame
health_data <- data.frame(
  height = numeric(0),
  weight = numeric(0),
  bmi = numeric(0)
)

# Open the data editor
health_data <- edit(health_data)
```

# 4. Data importation

R can import information from text files, spreadsheets, statistical software and databases.

## 4.1 Import a text file

```{r import-text, eval=FALSE}
# Read a text file from your computer
class_data <- read.table("class_data.txt", header = TRUE)

# Display the variable names
variable.names(class_data)

# Display the first and last rows
head(class_data)
tail(class_data)

# Select rows 5 to 10
class_data[5:10, ]
```

## 4.2 Import an Excel file

```{r import-excel, eval=FALSE}
# Install readxl once if it is not installed
install.packages("readxl")

# Import an Excel file
excel_data <- readxl::read_excel("class_data.xlsx")

# Display the first rows
head(excel_data)
```

## 4.3 Import data from statistical software

```{r import-statistical, eval=FALSE}
# Install haven once if it is not installed
install.packages("haven")

# Import an SPSS file
spss_data <- haven::read_sav("class_data.sav")

# Import a Stata file
stata_data <- haven::read_dta("class_data.dta")

# Import a SAS file
sas_data <- haven::read_sas("class_data.sas7bdat")
```

## 4.4 Import data from a database

```{r import-database, eval=FALSE}
# Install the packages needed for PostgreSQL
install.packages(c("DBI", "RPostgres"))

# Connect to your PostgreSQL database
connection <- DBI::dbConnect(
  RPostgres::Postgres(),
  dbname = "your_database",
  host = "localhost",
  port = 5432,
  user = "your_username",
  password = "your_password"
)

# List the tables in the database
DBI::dbListTables(connection)

# Read a table
database_data <- DBI::dbReadTable(connection, "students")

# Close the connection
DBI::dbDisconnect(connection)
```

## 4.5 Use a dataset already available in R

```{r built-in-data}
# List datasets available in R
data()

# Load the airquality dataset
data("airquality")

# Check its variables and structure
variable.names(airquality)
str(airquality)
head(airquality)
```

# 5. Exploring and describing data

We can use R to understand the size, structure and contents of a dataset.

```{r explore-data}
# Display the student dataset
student_data

# Check the summary of each variable
summary(student_data)

# Check the structure
str(student_data)

# Count rows and columns
nrow(student_data)
ncol(student_data)

# Count the number of weight values
length(student_data$weight)
```

## 5.1 Select rows and columns

```{r select-data}
# Select rows 2 to 4
student_data[2:4, ]

# Select only the weight column
student_data$weight

# Select the height column using its position
student_data[, 4]

# Select all columns except student_id
student_data[, -1]
```

## 5.2 Summary statistics

```{r summary-statistics}
# Summarize the weight variable
summary(student_data$weight)

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of height
mean(student_data$height)
sd(student_data$height)

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of weight
mean(student_data$weight)
sd(student_data$weight)

# Calculate the average of each row
apply(student_data[, c("height", "weight")], 1, mean)

# Calculate the standard deviation of each column
apply(student_data[, c("height", "weight")], 2, sd)
```

# 6. Comparing categories and numerical values

The iris dataset helps us compare flower measurements across species.

```{r iris-data}
# Load the iris dataset
data("iris")

# View the first rows
head(iris)

# Calculate the average petal length
mean(iris$Petal.Length)
```

## 6.1 Calculate statistics by group

```{r iris-groups}
# Average petal length for each species
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)

# Standard deviation for each species
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, sd)

# Full summary for each species
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, summary)
```

## 6.2 Boxplot

A boxplot compares a numerical variable across categories.

```{r iris-boxplot}
# Compare sepal length across flower species
boxplot(
  Sepal.Length ~ Species,
  data = iris,
  main = "Sepal Length by Flower Species",
  xlab = "Species",
  ylab = "Sepal length"
)
```

# 7. Comparing two categorical variables

The built-in UCBAdmissions dataset contains university admission information.

```{r admissions-data}
# Convert the dataset into a data frame
admissions <- data.frame(UCBAdmissions)

# View the first rows
head(admissions)

# Create a table of gender and admission outcome
admission_table <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = admissions)
admission_table

# Calculate admission proportions for each gender
prop.table(admission_table, 1)
```

# 8. Bar charts

Bar charts help compare values across categories.

```{r bar-chart}
# Create a small dataset of monthly sales
sales <- data.frame(
  Product_A = c(100, 120),
  Product_B = c(50, 60),
  Product_C = c(70, 90),
  Product_D = c(80, 75)
)

# Draw bars side by side
barplot(
  as.matrix(sales),
  beside = TRUE,
  main = "Product Sales Comparison",
  ylab = "Sales"
)
```

```{r second-bar-chart}
# Create another dataset for four branches
branch_sales <- data.frame(
  Branch_A = c(10, 20, 30, 25),
  Branch_B = c(15, 25, 35, 20),
  Branch_C = c(20, 30, 25, 40)
)

# Compare sales across branches
barplot(
  as.matrix(branch_sales),
  main = "Sales by Branch",
  ylab = "Sales"
)
```

# 9. Scatter plots and correlation

A scatter plot helps us see how two numerical variables move together.

```{r scatter-plots}
# Plot weight against height
plot(weight ~ height, data = student_data)

# Create the same plot using column names
plot(student_data$height, student_data$weight)

# Add a title to the graph
plot(
  student_data$height,
  student_data$weight,
  main = "Relationship Between Height and Weight",
  xlab = "Height (cm)",
  ylab = "Weight (kg)"
)
```

```{r correlation}
# Calculate the correlation between height and weight
cor(student_data$height, student_data$weight)
```

# 10. Linear models

A linear model helps us examine the relationship between two numerical variables.

```{r linear-model}
# Estimate weight using height
weight_model <- lm(weight ~ height, data = student_data)

# Display the model results
summary(weight_model)
```

```{r linear-model-plot}
# Plot the observations
plot(
  weight ~ height,
  data = student_data,
  main = "Height and Weight"
)

# Add the fitted straight line
abline(weight_model)
```

```{r model-diagnostics}
# Display diagnostic plots for the model
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(weight_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r smooth-line}
# Add a smooth line to the scatter plot
plot(weight ~ height, data = student_data)
abline(weight_model)
lines(
  lowess(student_data$height, student_data$weight),
  col = "pink"
)
```

# 11. Data management: creating new variables

We can calculate a new variable using existing columns.

```{r create-bmi}
# Calculate BMI using height in metres
student_data$BMI <- round(
  student_data$weight / (student_data$height / 100)^2,
  digits = 2
)

# Display the dataset with BMI
student_data

# Display the first and last rows
head(student_data, n = 3)
tail(student_data, n = 3)

# Summarize BMI
summary(student_data$BMI)

# Display BMI values in a stem-and-leaf plot
stem(student_data$BMI)
```

# 12. Working with dates

R can store dates and calculate the time between them.

```{r dates}
# Get today's date
today <- Sys.Date()
today

# Display the month, day and year
format(today, format = "%B %d %Y")

# Display the day of the week
format(today, format = "%A")

# Calculate the difference between two dates
course_start <- as.Date("2026-10-18")
course_end <- as.Date("2026-12-18")

course_end - course_start
```

# 13. Subsetting and managing data

We will use a fictional survey about leadership and decision-making.

Participants answered five questions using this scale:

- 1 = Strongly disagree
- 2 = Disagree
- 3 = Neither agree nor disagree
- 4 = Agree
- 5 = Strongly agree

```{r leadership-data}
# Create the survey information
manager_id <- 1:6
country <- c("Rwanda", "Rwanda", "Kenya", "Kenya", "Uganda", "Uganda")
gender <- c("M", "F", "F", "M", "F", "M")
age <- c(29, 42, 31, 38, 99, 34)

# Answers to five leadership questions
q1 <- c(5, 3, 4, 3, 2, 4)
q2 <- c(4, 5, 5, 3, 2, 4)
q3 <- c(5, 2, 4, 4, 1, 5)
q4 <- c(5, 5, 4, NA, 2, 4)
q5 <- c(4, 5, 3, NA, 1, 5)

# Combine the information into a data frame
leadership <- data.frame(
  manager_id, country, gender, age,
  q1, q2, q3, q4, q5
)

leadership
str(leadership)
names(leadership)
```

## 13.1 Handle missing values

In this example, age `99` means the participant did not provide their age.

```{r leadership-missing}
# Replace 99 with NA
leadership$age[leadership$age == 99] <- NA

# Check missing values
is.na(leadership)

# Remove rows that contain missing values
complete_leadership <- na.omit(leadership)

complete_leadership
```

## 13.2 Create age groups

```{r age-groups}
# Create an empty age category column
leadership$age_group <- NA_character_

# Categorize participants by age
leadership$age_group[leadership$age < 35] <- "Young"

leadership$age_group[
  leadership$age >= 35 & leadership$age <= 75
] <- "Middle aged"

leadership$age_group[leadership$age > 75] <- "Elder"

leadership
```

## 13.3 Combine the five question scores

```{r combine-scores}
# Calculate the total score for each participant
leadership$total_score <- rowSums(
  leadership[, c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5")],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

leadership
```

## 13.4 Sort the data

```{r sort-leadership}
# Show the order of participants by age
order(leadership$age)

# Sort participants from youngest to oldest
sorted_leadership <- leadership[order(leadership$age), ]

sorted_leadership
```

## 13.5 Merge two data frames

```{r merge-data}
# Create another dataset with the same manager IDs
department_info <- data.frame(
  manager_id = 1:6,
  department = c("Finance", "HR", "IT", "Operations", "Finance", "IT")
)

# Join both datasets using manager_id
leadership_full <- merge(
  leadership,
  department_info,
  by = "manager_id"
)

leadership_full
```

## 13.6 Select and remove columns

```{r select-columns}
# Select only the five question columns
question_data <- leadership[, c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5")]
question_data

# Remove manager_id and country
reduced_data <- leadership[, -c(1, 2)]
reduced_data
```

## 13.7 Access columns using different methods

```{r access-columns}
# Access the age column using $
leadership$age

# Access the fourth column using its position
leadership[[4]]

# Access selected rows
leadership[c(1, 3, 5), ]
```

## 13.8 Filter observations

```{r filter-data}
# Select participants who are male and older than 30
male_managers <- subset(
  leadership,
  gender == "M" & age > 30
)

male_managers

# Select participants aged 35 or older or younger than 30
selected_managers <- subset(
  leadership,
  age >= 35 | age < 30,
  select = c(q1, q2, q3, q4, q5)
)

selected_managers
```
